chapter_theme: Kanjamalai Siddhar's song is Vedantic in vocabulary and prohibitive in form: the world is imagination and dream, the body comes from ego-impurity and is worked by five, and the stanzas pile up negative imperatives, do not argue, do not crave what has not come, do not fall for women, do not trust learning, do not circle temples, against one positive counsel, to still the running mind in the open space of nada's end, hold to the guru's word and feet, and find the self-luminous within the very play of the faculties. Rites, tattva-lists and tapas are a heap and a burden; silence and jnana-inquiry are the essence.
structure_note: A head unit (2267) and twenty-four stanzas of four short lines, each line ending in one rhyme (-ள்ளு, -ாரம், -ாதே, -ந்து) and the fourth usually carrying the point. 2268 to 2275 set the doctrine (the world as maya and dream, the body as ego's product, the guru as the limit); 2276 to 2283 are mostly prohibitions (-ாதே) against company, dispute, craving, women, learning and the belly; 2284 to 2291 return to the soul, the guru's word, the pairs of opposites, speech, the body and the temple, ending on the self-light within the faculties' play. 2292 (ch117) closes the song. Tradition names a Kanjamalaiyan among Tirumular's disciples (Tirumanthiram 1443); whether this song's poet is that figure or a later namesake from the Kanjamalai hill near Salem is not decidable from the text.

2267.reading: The awareness that is perfect, full bliss: the ever-blissful feet of Siva, the Supreme Brahman.
2267.nuance: A two-line head or invocation, with Vedanta's names (பரிபூரணம், சிவபரப்பிரமம், சதானந்தம்) given at once to Siva's feet; the song's vocabulary is announced here.

2268.reading: Think on the Supreme that is yours by right; throw off the bewilderment of the world made by maya; utter the rare name of Siva; take up with love the service of Siva's devotees.
2268.nuance: Four imperatives on one rhyme (உள்ளு, தள்ளு, விள்ளு, கொள்ளு); the two inward ones (thinking the Supreme, rejecting maya) are paired with two outward and devotional ones (the name, service to devotees), which the song will not repeat but does not retract.

2269.reading: Inquiry into base worldly life is small pleasure that turns to sorrow, a great horror; the inquiry that is certain is the essence of stainless jnana-Vedanta; that is the essence.
2269.nuance: விசாரம் is used twice, for brooding on worldly affairs and for the inquiry of Vedanta; the stanza does not oppose thinking to not-thinking but one object of thought to another. சாரமே சாரம் doubles the word for essence.

2270.reading: The world is imagination, an expanse produced by the inner faculties, a dream, an Indra's net; if on that day it appears so, that is favourable to the subtle.
2270.nuance: அந்தக்கரணம், the inner faculties (mind, intellect, ego, will), are made the producers of the world, which is Vedanta's idealism; இந்த்ரசாலம் is the conjuror's show. The last line is obscure: perhaps that once the world has appeared as dream, the subtle is in reach. 2291 returns to the faculties and says their play cannot be pushed away.

2271.reading: The world is trifling; if you go along with it, it gives you only a little; the heart that stands fixed in grace, on that day there is nothing equal to it, nothing equal, the ... of true knowledge.
2271.nuance: பொஞ்சம் in the last line is unknown, perhaps a rhyme-word coined against கொஞ்சம், or a corruption; the stanza's sense, the world's little against grace's incomparable, does not depend on it.

2272.reading: Ruin came from ego; throw desire, the root, far off with its bundle; the house of bliss that cannot be contained, on that day the dissolution of mind that strikes joins of itself.
2272.nuance: மனோலயம், the dissolution of mind, is a yogic and Vedantic term for the state in which the mind subsides; the stanza says it comes of itself (தானாக) once desire is thrown out, so the positive state is not made but allowed.

2273.reading: What are the heaps of tattvas? What are the rites called the sastras of attainment? With devotion that does not forget, when you see the guru's feet, then it will be known.
2273.nuance: தத்துவக் குப்பைகள், heaps or rubbish of tattvas, dismisses the Saiva Siddhanta enumerations of thirty-six; சித்தி சாத்திரம் may be the texts of ritual attainment or the Siddhars' own siddhi manuals. Both are replaced by the guru's feet, seen, and the knowing is deferred to that moment (அப்போது).

2274.reading: There are no far distances; to try to touch and catch it is great trouble; trusting the word of the causal teacher and fixing it in the mind, one can see the limit.
2274.nuance: The Supreme is not far and yet cannot be grasped by effort; the way is the guru's word held in mind. காரண தேசிகன், the teacher who is the cause, may be the human guru or Siva as guru. எல்லை, the limit or bound, is the end of the search, not the Supreme's boundary.

2275.reading: The body came from the impurity of ego; in it five sit and do their work by rule; it is a maya that will vanish unseen; I have told you well the formula tried by hand, the means.
2275.nuance: ஆணவம் is the first of Saiva Siddhanta's three malas, the soul's root darkness; the body is its product. ஐவர், the five, are the senses or the elements, tradition giving both. கைகண்ட சூத்திரம், a formula proven by hand, is the alchemist's and physician's phrase, here used for a doctrine.

2276.reading: Do not hold to the company of fools; do not die by the derangement of lust for women; do not fall for display; while the nectar of jnana is there, do not drink poison.
2276.nuance: The stanza's four prohibitions end on the strongest contrast, nectar at hand and poison chosen, which is Tirumular's figure for the ritualist beside the knower.

2277.reading: Do not dispute saying 'I'; do not throw out arguments and hiss in anger; the bond called flesh does not change; if it goes, by your own oath, your mind will not be done with even in death.
2277.nuance: The second half is hard: ஊனென்ற பாசம் மாறாதே may be a statement, that attachment to the flesh does not change, or another prohibition, do not change it. The last line seems to say that if life goes with the mind still disputing, the mind's state outlasts the body; உன்னாணை, 'by your oath', is an asseveration.

2278.reading: Do not push away what has come; do not hold vain desire for what has not come; do not leap about at the mind's will; stay still like a picture and do not utter anything.
2278.nuance: சித்திரம் போல, like a painting, is the stillness of the yogi; the stanza's equanimity toward what comes and does not come is the Kural's ஊழ் chapter in a Siddhar's mouth.

2279.reading: Body-attachment and the bonds of birth: that thing, the small pleasure, is a stinking smell; the Vedanta that is one's portion, if you contemplate the thing, is yours.
2279.nuance: சிச்சீர்க்கந்தம் joins the exclamation of disgust (சீ) to கந்தம், smell; பாகமதான may be the Vedanta that has ripened or that is one's share. The contrast is between the pleasure that attaches to the body and the knowledge that becomes one's own (சொந்தம்) by contemplation.

2280.reading: Desire for women will not do; if that delusion takes hold it does not go even a little; do not die in fear at Yama's hand; do not burn in the fire called wicked desire-bonds.
2280.nuance: ஆசாபாசம், desire-bond, is a compound the Siddhars favour, treating craving and the bond it makes as one thing; it is a fire here where 2276 made it poison.

2281.reading: Crossing the delusion of learning, destroying the dross of thinking 'we have learned it all', lying in the heat of words, desire spreading into the subtle beyond the subtle...
2281.nuance: A chain of participles without a finite verb; it may run into 2282, where the mind is to be caught and set in the open space. சூட்சாதி சூட்சம், the subtle of subtles, is the Supreme; the ஆசை that spreads toward it is the one desire the song allows. The stanza mocks the learned (கற்றோம் என்று) in the Siddhars' usual way.

2282.reading: The thought that runs about: catch it without letting it run, gather it and set it right; seek, and fit it to the arrow; set it within the wide open space of nada's end.
2282.nuance: அம்பு, the arrow, recurs in 2287 (அம்பு பூணும்); tradition reads it as the fixed inward gaze or the straight breath. நாதாந்த வெட்டவெளி, the bare open space at the end of sound, is where the mind is to be lodged; the stanza is the song's one positive method, framed in the same imperatives as its prohibitions.

2283.reading: Do not wander for the span-sized belly; do not be bewildered by daily anxiety; do not be melted in the forge of ego; for you the release that is bliss, stand firm in that.
2283.nuance: அது நிலையாதே can be the fourth prohibition's form carrying a positive sense ('stand in that'), or a statement that otherwise release will not abide (நிலையாது). The சாண் வயிறு, the span of belly for which one roams, is the Siddhars' standing figure for the whole economy of livelihood.

2284.reading: The soul that is the egoist is destroyed by its ignorance; if it thinks of tapas it reaches awareness; and if it holds that state, it becomes the form of Shakti too.
2284.nuance: அபிமானி, the one who identifies, is the soul as ego; the stanza gives three stages, destruction by ignorance, awareness (போதம்) by tapas, and Shakti's form by holding the state. That the end is Shakti's form and not Siva's is unusual in a song whose head unit (2267) is to Siva's feet; the text does not explain it.

2285.reading: Say only what the good guru said; if it is the quest of the pillar, stand in the state of fire; let go of the sects of your own time; eat, and take yourself as being of its own nature.
2285.nuance: தம்பம், the pillar, is tradition's name for the spine or the central channel, and வன்னி நிலை, the fire state, the fire centre at the base or navel; so read, the stanza is a yoga instruction. விள்ளு was 'utter' in 2268 and may be 'split off, let go' here; தற்சமயங்கள் may be present-day sects or the sects of the self. உண்டு, 'having eaten', may be literal or the enjoyment of the state.

2286.reading: Touching sorrow and joy, burning all those pairs so that the rust is gone, then letting go of attachment, saying not one thing, leaving behind the greatness of the end...
2286.nuance: Another participial chain without a close. தொந்தங்கள் are the pairs of opposites (dvandva) of Vedanta; துருசு is rust or dross. அந்தம் பெருமையை விட்டு may be giving up even the pride of having reached the end, or the greatness of the six ends (ஆறந்தம்); the text does not fix it.

2287.reading: What does talk bring to light? Talking and talking is nothing but error, is it not? Because of ... one wears the arrow; what is needed is a flawless inquiry of jnana.
2287.nuance: வாச்சுதலால் is obscure (perhaps 'by its coming about'); அம்பு பூணும் repeats the arrow of 2282. The contrast between பேச்சு (talk) and விசாரணை (inquiry) is the song's own: inquiry is the one use of thought it keeps (2269).

2288.reading: The body is impermanent; in it, infatuation is not contained by desire alone; if one stays alone, that enjoyment, standing as oneself alone, is Siva-yoga.
2288.nuance: தனித்திருந்தால், staying alone, is both solitude and the standing-as-one (தானாகி நிற்பது) that the stanza calls Siva-yoga; the enjoyment (போகம்) desire sought is redefined as the yogi's. The second line is compressed; ஆசையும் ஒன்றால் may mean that desire, being one thing, does not contain the infatuation it breeds.

2289.reading: Give no room to the desire that wants; do not get bound within the pains of the body; do not take birth again; do not let go of love at the feet of the guru-teacher.
2289.nuance: Four -ாதே lines, the last turned positive by a double negative: the one thing not to give up is love for the guru's feet, the song's constant positive (2273, 2274, 2285).

2290.reading: Crores upon crores of austerities, and the japas recited going round that temple: are they not a toil of births? They are the defilements of sorrow that come upon one before one does this.
2290.nuance: பாடான பவங்கள் is read as births that are toil, or the toil of births; the austerities and temple japa are made part of the round of birth and not its cure. இது பண்ணுமுன், 'before doing this', seems to refer to the inquiry of 2287, so that the rites belong to the time before one knows. அமலங்கள் is read as மலங்கள் with a prefixed அ; it could also be 'the stainless', which would reverse the sense, but the line's துன்ப tells against it.

2291.reading: The play of the inner faculties: no one can push it away, whatever the effort; what stands joined to it is bondage; within it, appearing without appearing, is the self-luminous.
2291.nuance: The stanza qualifies 2270: the faculties' conjuring cannot be stopped, only unjoined from (தொந்தித்து, being coupled, is the bondage), and the self-light (சுயம்பிரகாசம்) is found within the play, not after it ends. தோன்றாமற் தோன்றும், appearing without appearing, is the Siddhars' formula for what is seen without being an object.

links.note: Kanjamalai calls the inquiry of stainless jnana-Vedanta the one essence; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will leave all Vedanta and the Veda behind and stay alone in absorption. If both mean Vedanta as a body of teaching, the one keeps what the other discards; if Kanjamalai means the knowledge and Pattiragiriyar the texts, they agree. The tension holds on the first reading.

2270 makes the world a dream and a conjuror's show produced by the inner faculties; 2291 says no one can push the faculties' play away, that bondage is being coupled to it, and that the self-light appears within it. The second stanza keeps the first's doctrine and removes its hope of stopping the show.

The Kural says that giving up insatiable craving at once gives a nature that never shifts; Kanjamalai says that when desire is thrown out root and bundle, the dissolution of mind joins of itself. Both make the positive state follow immediately and without further effort from the removal of craving.

Tirumular's true guru, by giving his feet, grants self-knowledge, brings the soul beyond the tattvas and quells the bonds; Kanjamalai says the heaps of tattvas and the rites are nothing and that seeing the guru's feet is when it becomes known. The feet do in both what the tattva-lists cannot.

Tirumular says the Lord's servants, the Siva-yogis and the eminent do not want ritual works, they want love; Kanjamalai asks what the rites called sastras of attainment are and answers with unforgetting devotion and the guru's feet. Both set bhakti against rite from inside a tradition that prescribes rite.

Tirumular's Lord is far off yet near to those who love well; Kanjamalai says there are no far distances, that grasping him by effort is great trouble, and that trusting the guru's word brings one to the limit. In both the distance is not spatial and is closed by trust, not by reaching.

Sangili's five persons join to rule and build the body as the Gingee fort; Kanjamalai's body comes from ego-impurity and five sit in it and work by rule. The five (elements or senses) govern the body in both, and both poets call the account a secret told plainly.

Tirumular's ritualist eats bitter things while ghee, milk and curd stand at hand; Kanjamalai says do not drink poison while the nectar of jnana is there. The same figure of the worthless chosen over the precious at hand, Tirumular's for the karmi beside the jnani, Kanjamalai's for display and lust beside knowledge.

Tirumular says that though many speak of the things to join with the Pure One, the one who conquers the senses and quickly ends dispute knows him; Kanjamalai says do not dispute saying 'I', do not throw out arguments. Both make the end of argument a condition of knowing, not a result.

Tirumular's knowers perceive Siva's fragrance in the soul 'steady as a painting'; Kanjamalai says stay still like a picture and utter nothing. The painted figure is the still yogi in both, and both pair the stillness with silence.

The Kural says what is not yours will not stay however guarded and what is yours will not leave though thrown away; Kanjamalai says do not push away what has come and do not crave what has not. The Kural's chapter is on ஊழ், fate; Kanjamalai draws from the same fact the yogi's equanimity rather than a doctrine of fate.

Sivavakkiyar's book-carriers babble lies and do not know where one dies and is born; Kanjamalai says to cross the delusion of learning and destroy the dross of 'we have learned it all'. Both aim at the pride of the learned, not at learning as such, and both set an inner knowledge against it.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will see the waste mind that wanders by the five senses' paths burn and fall; Kanjamalai tells the listener to catch the thought that runs about and set it in the open space of nada's end. The same running mind, to be burnt in the one and lodged in the other.

Tirumular's soul, freed of the malas, sees itself and becomes Hara, beyond the tattvas, which he calls Vedanta's truth; Kanjamalai's egoist soul is destroyed by ignorance, reaches awareness by tapas and becomes Shakti's form by holding the state. Both run from the bound soul to divine form, Tirumular's ending in Siva and Kanjamalai's in Shakti.

Tirumular's Siva-yoga is to know the conscient and the non-conscient, enter the yoga of tapas and become one's own light; Kanjamalai's Siva-yoga is to stay alone and stand as oneself alone in an impermanent body. Both define Siva-yoga by a state of the self rather than by posture or breath.

The Kural says the moment attachment ends it cuts off births; Kanjamalai says give no room to desire, do not get bound in the body's pains, do not take birth again. Both make the end of craving and the end of birth one event; Kanjamalai adds the guru's feet as the thing to hold instead.

Sivavakkiyar counts the flowers he threw, the mantras he recited into the void and the times he circled Siva's temples; Kanjamalai calls crores of austerities and the japa recited round the temple a toil of births. Both count the acts to show that counting them is all they amount to.

Tirumular says those who do great tapas without forgetting win the greatness of ending birth; Kanjamalai says crores upon crores of tapas, with temple japa, are a toil of births and the defilements of sorrow. If தவங்கள் in 2290 means tapas as such, the two claims about what tapas does to birth are opposite; if it means only the ritual austerities counted and performed, Tirumular's unforgetting tapas is a different thing.

The Tirumanthiram names a Kanjamalaiyan among those who examined the root chariyai, the outward service of the Lord that is 'the life of pure Saivam'; the song under Kanjamalai Siddhar's name calls the japa recited round the temple a toil of births. If the two names are one person, the texts give him opposite valuations of temple service; if not, the tension is between the lineage's founder and a later namesake. Either way the claim that chariyai is the life of Saivam and the claim that temple rounds are a burden of births do not stand together.

source_issues: 2267 is printed as an unnumbered head unit (u1), two lines where the stanzas have four; it is the song's invocation and may be a later editor's heading.
2271 line 4: பொஞ்சம் is unknown; probably a rhyme-word forced against கொஞ்சம், possibly corrupt.
2272 line 1: கேடு-முதல் and other hyphens in this work mark the caesura between the half-lines, not compounds; 2274 and 2277 have the hyphen replaced by a comma.
2281 line 2: கற்றோ மென்று றெண்ணுங் has a doubled ற (மென்று றெண்ணும்); read மென்று எண்ணும்.
2283 line 4: கானந்த முத்தி is ஆனந்த முத்தி with the initial க் carried over from உனக்கு by sandhi; printed as one word.
2281 and 2286 are participial chains with no finite verb; each may continue into the next stanza or be incomplete.
2290 line 4: அமலங்கள் is read as மலங்கள் (defilements) with a prothetic அ; the alternative sense 'stainless ones' is possible but inconsistent with துன்ப.
